Clustering · Customer Segmentation

Selecting a Customer Segmentation Method

An empirical evaluation of RFM rules, K-means, Gaussian mixture, Ward, DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, and spectral clustering

52configurations across 7 methods
4,966customers in the shared matrix
6months of out-of-time evidence
5RFM segments recommended
Abstract
  • Compares seven ways to segment an online retailer's customers: RFM rules and six clustering families (K-means, Gaussian mixture, Ward, DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, spectral), across 52 configurations
  • Every method gets the same 4,966 customers, features and scaling, built from 19 months of transactions
  • The final six months are held back to test whether segments still differ in later purchasing behavior
  • Methods are judged on structure, stability, later behavior, interpretability, deployability and sensitivity to preprocessing, with no single composite score
  • DBSCAN and HDBSCAN produced no usable segmentation under the grids tested
  • Clustering assignments were fragile: the best K-means configuration kept an adjusted Rand index of only 0.158 when preprocessing changed, while RFM was unchanged (1.000)
  • Five-segment RFM rules selected: the only method to clear the business gates at every tolerance, with the strongest later-behavior differentiation (η² = 0.262) and the largest minimum segment (14.5% of customers)
  • The six clustering families added complexity without beating a well-built baseline

01Introduction

  • Goal: choose one segmentation method for periodic customer classification and downstream campaign testing, balancing economic value against operating burden
  • Analytical question: which approach produces customer groups that remain useful when evaluated against subsequent purchasing behavior, not just against a clustering score
  • Research question: how do rule-based, centroid, probabilistic, hierarchical, density-based, and graph-based methods compare when given identical customer data and identical decision criteria
  • Data: Online Retail II1, two years of transactions from a UK-based non-store retailer
  • Decision boundary: this study selects a method and proposes campaign hypotheses; it does not estimate the incremental effect of any campaign, and each proposed action requires a subsequent experiment
  • Findings describe associations in historical purchasing behavior and are not presented as causal effects
  • Independent portfolio study using a public dataset; it does not represent work completed for an employer or client
1 Chen, D. (2019). Online Retail II [Dataset]. UCI Machine Learning Repository. https://doi.org/10.24432/C5CG6D.

Initialize Environment¶

  • NumPy and pandas for data manipulation; matplotlib and seaborn for visualization
  • scikit-learn for preprocessing (robust scaling), clustering (K-means, Gaussian mixture, Ward, DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, spectral), and evaluation (silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz, adjusted Rand index)
  • Study constants fixed before any model was fit: random seed 42, six-month holdout, and a candidate range of two through ten clusters

02Data Readiness

  • Asked whether the transaction history was reliable enough to support customer-level segmentation before any feature was built
  • Both workbook sheets were combined and the raw source preserved, so cleaning decisions could be measured rather than hidden
  • Study conventions were fixed in advance: one row per identified customer, unknown customers excluded from modeling, and cancellations retained as engineered behavior rather than netted against sales

Online Retail II Dataset¶

  • Transactions from a UK-based non-store online retailer specializing in unique all-occasion giftware
  • 1,067,371 rows across two sheets covering 2009-12-01 through 2011-12-09, 738 observed days (Table 1)
  • Fields: invoice number, stock code, description, quantity, invoice date, unit price, customer ID, and country
In [2]:
# Load Transaction Workbook
def load_retail_workbook(path: Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    if not path.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f'Workbook not found at {path}. Download Online Retail II '            'from the UCI Machine Learning Repository and place it in the data folder.'
        )

    workbook = pd.ExcelFile(path)
    frames = []

    for sheet_name in workbook.sheet_names:
        sheet = pd.read_excel(path, sheet_name=sheet_name)
        sheet['SourceSheet'] = sheet_name
        frames.append(sheet)

    transactions = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)
    transactions.columns = [str(column).strip() for column in transactions.columns]
    return transactions

raw_transactions = load_retail_workbook(DATA_PATH)
print(f'Rows loaded: {len(raw_transactions):,}')
print(f'Workbook sheets: {raw_transactions["SourceSheet"].nunique():,}')
display(raw_transactions.head())

Initial Data Audit¶

  • 53,628 invoices and 5,942 identified customers in the full history (Table 2)
  • 243,007 rows (22.8%) carry no customer ID and cannot be linked to a customer, so they are excluded from customer-level modeling
  • Cancellations appear on 19,494 rows (1.8%); 22,950 rows (2.2%) carry a nonpositive quantity and 6,207 (0.6%) a nonpositive unit price
  • No invalid transaction dates, so the date range supports a clean development and holdout design (Table 3)
In [3]:
# Initial Data Audit
def normalize_columns(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    aliases = {
        'Invoice': 'InvoiceNo',
        'Customer ID': 'CustomerID',
        'Price': 'UnitPrice',
    }
    return frame.rename(columns=aliases).copy()

transactions = normalize_columns(raw_transactions)
required_columns = {
    'InvoiceNo', 'StockCode', 'Description', 'Quantity',
    'InvoiceDate', 'UnitPrice', 'CustomerID', 'Country'
}
missing_columns = sorted(required_columns.difference(transactions.columns))
if missing_columns:
    raise ValueError(f'Missing required columns: {missing_columns}')

transactions['InvoiceDate'] = pd.to_datetime(transactions['InvoiceDate'], errors='coerce')
transactions['InvoiceNo'] = transactions['InvoiceNo'].astype('string').str.strip()
transactions['is_cancellation'] = transactions['InvoiceNo'].str.upper().str.startswith('C', na=False)
transactions['line_value'] = transactions['Quantity'] * transactions['UnitPrice']

audit = pd.DataFrame({
    'Metric': [
        'Transaction rows',
        'Observed invoices',
        'Identified customers',
        'Rows missing CustomerID',
        'Cancellation rows',
        'Rows with nonpositive quantity',
        'Rows with nonpositive unit price',
        'Rows with invalid transaction date',
    ],
    'Value': [
        len(transactions),
        transactions['InvoiceNo'].nunique(dropna=True),
        transactions['CustomerID'].nunique(dropna=True),
        transactions['CustomerID'].isna().sum(),
        transactions['is_cancellation'].sum(),
        transactions['Quantity'].le(0).sum(),
        transactions['UnitPrice'].le(0).sum(),
        transactions['InvoiceDate'].isna().sum(),
    ],
})
audit['Share of rows'] = audit['Value'] / len(transactions)
display(audit.style.format({'Value': '{:,.0f}', 'Share of rows': '{:.1%}'}))

date_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    'First observed transaction': [transactions['InvoiceDate'].min()],
    'Last observed transaction': [transactions['InvoiceDate'].max()],
    'Observed days': [(transactions['InvoiceDate'].max() - transactions['InvoiceDate'].min()).days],
})

03Study Design

  • Segments were constructed only from development-period transactions, with the final six months reserved to evaluate subsequent behavior
  • Holding the later period back prevents future transactions from influencing segment definitions
  • The holdout was used to compare candidate solutions, which makes it a validation period rather than an untouched final test

Development & Holdout Periods¶

  • Development: 745,435 rows, 39,069 invoices, 5,031 customers, through 2011-06-08 (Table 4)
  • Holdout: 321,936 rows, 14,559 invoices, 3,523 customers, 2011-06-09 through 2011-12-09
  • The cutoff falls six months before the last observed transaction, so the holdout spans a partial June rather than six whole calendar months
In [4]:
# Development & Holdout Periods
last_observed_date = transactions['InvoiceDate'].max().normalize()
holdout_start = (last_observed_date - pd.DateOffset(months=HOLDOUT_MONTHS)).normalize()

transactions['study_period'] = np.where(
    transactions['InvoiceDate'] < holdout_start,
    'Development',
    'Holdout',
)
transactions.loc[transactions['InvoiceDate'].isna(), 'study_period'] = 'Invalid date'

period_summary = (
    transactions.groupby('study_period', dropna=False)
    .agg(
        rows=('InvoiceNo', 'size'),
        invoices=('InvoiceNo', 'nunique'),
        customers=('CustomerID', 'nunique'),
        first_date=('InvoiceDate', 'min'),
        last_date=('InvoiceDate', 'max'),
    )
    .reset_index()
)
display(period_summary.style.format({'rows': '{:,.0f}', 'invoices': '{:,.0f}', 'customers': '{:,.0f}'}))
print(f'Provisional holdout start: {holdout_start:%Y-%m-%d}')

04Customer Feature Construction

  • Converted the transaction history into one row per identified customer, using development-period activity only
  • Three field roles kept separate: modeling features (behavior available at the cutoff), profiling fields (used to explain segments, never to create them), and holdout outcomes (never used to construct or select a solution)
  • Coverage convention: every identified customer with at least one valid positive-value development order was retained, so one-time customers remain part of the business population

Transaction Rules¶

  • Positive sales and cancellation behavior were represented separately, so negative quantities never silently offset valid purchases
  • 574,680 development rows (77.1%) link to a customer; 561,011 (75.3%) qualify as valid positive sales (Table 5)
  • 16,981 rows (2.3%) are returns or cancellations, retained as behavioral signal rather than discarded
In [5]:
# Transaction Rule Audit
development = transactions.loc[
    transactions['study_period'].eq('Development')
].copy()

development['has_customer_id'] = development['CustomerID'].notna()
development['is_positive_sale'] = (
    development['has_customer_id']
    & development['InvoiceDate'].notna()
    & ~development['is_cancellation']
    & development['Quantity'].gt(0)
    & development['UnitPrice'].gt(0)
)
development['is_return_or_cancellation'] = (
    development['is_cancellation']
    | development['Quantity'].lt(0)
)

rule_audit = pd.DataFrame({
    'Population': [
        'Development-period rows',
        'Rows linked to a customer',
        'Valid positive-sale rows',
        'Return or cancellation rows',
        'Rows excluded from positive sales',
    ],
    'Rows': [
        len(development),
        development['has_customer_id'].sum(),
        development['is_positive_sale'].sum(),
        development['is_return_or_cancellation'].sum(),
        (~development['is_positive_sale']).sum(),
    ],
})
rule_audit['Share'] = rule_audit['Rows'] / len(development)

display(
    rule_audit.style
    .format({'Rows': '{:,.0f}', 'Share': '{:.1%}'})
    .bar(subset=['Share'], color='#9ecae1', vmin=0, vmax=1)
    .set_properties(subset=['Population'], **{'text-align': 'left'})
    .set_properties(subset=['Rows', 'Share'], **{'text-align': 'right'})
    .set_table_styles([
        {'selector': 'th', 'props': [('text-align', 'left')]},
    ])
)

Engineered Customer Behaviors¶

  • Five business dimensions captured: recency, frequency, economic value, product behavior, and relationship behavior
  • Features were kept interpretable before any transformation or scaling
  • 4,966 customers qualified with at least one valid positive-value development order (Table 6)
  • Purchase-cadence measures (average and standard deviation of days between orders) were computed for profiling only, since they are undefined for single-order customers
In [6]:
# Customer Feature Table
positive_sales = development.loc[development['is_positive_sale']].copy()
positive_sales['CustomerID'] = positive_sales['CustomerID'].astype('string')
positive_sales['purchase_date'] = positive_sales['InvoiceDate'].dt.normalize()

order_level = (
    positive_sales.groupby(['CustomerID', 'InvoiceNo'], as_index=False)
    .agg(
        order_date=('InvoiceDate', 'min'),
        order_revenue=('line_value', 'sum'),
        order_units=('Quantity', 'sum'),
        order_skus=('StockCode', 'nunique'),
    )
)

customer_core = (
    positive_sales.groupby('CustomerID')
    .agg(
        first_purchase=('InvoiceDate', 'min'),
        last_purchase=('InvoiceDate', 'max'),
        active_days=('purchase_date', 'nunique'),
        unique_skus=('StockCode', 'nunique'),
        total_revenue=('line_value', 'sum'),
        total_units=('Quantity', 'sum'),
        primary_country=('Country', lambda values: values.mode().iloc[0] if not values.mode().empty else pd.NA),
    )
)

order_features = (
    order_level.groupby('CustomerID')
    .agg(
        order_count=('InvoiceNo', 'nunique'),
        average_order_value=('order_revenue', 'mean'),
        median_order_value=('order_revenue', 'median'),
        average_units_per_order=('order_units', 'mean'),
        average_skus_per_order=('order_skus', 'mean'),
    )
)

customer_features = customer_core.join(order_features, how='inner')
customer_features['recency_days'] = (
    holdout_start - customer_features['last_purchase'].dt.normalize()
).dt.days
customer_features['tenure_days'] = (
    customer_features['last_purchase'].dt.normalize()
    - customer_features['first_purchase'].dt.normalize()
).dt.days

customer_features = customer_features.reset_index()
print(f'Eligible development-period customers: {len(customer_features):,}')
display(customer_features.head())

# Purchase Cadence & Cancellation Behavior
def summarize_purchase_cadence(customer_orders: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
    order_dates = (
        customer_orders['order_date']
        .dt.normalize()
        .drop_duplicates()
        .sort_values()
    )
    gaps = order_dates.diff().dt.days.dropna()
    return pd.Series({
        'average_days_between_orders': gaps.mean(),
        'sd_days_between_orders': gaps.std(),
    })

cadence_features = (
    order_level.groupby('CustomerID', group_keys=False)
    .apply(summarize_purchase_cadence)
    .reset_index()
)

linked_activity = development.loc[development['has_customer_id']].copy()
linked_activity['CustomerID'] = linked_activity['CustomerID'].astype('string')
invoice_behavior = (
    linked_activity.groupby(['CustomerID', 'InvoiceNo'], as_index=False)
    .agg(is_return_or_cancellation=('is_return_or_cancellation', 'max'))
)
cancellation_features = (
    invoice_behavior.groupby('CustomerID')
    .agg(
        observed_invoice_count=('InvoiceNo', 'nunique'),
        cancellation_invoice_count=('is_return_or_cancellation', 'sum'),
    )
    .assign(
        cancellation_rate=lambda frame: (
            frame['cancellation_invoice_count'] / frame['observed_invoice_count']
        )
    )
    .reset_index()
)

customer_features = (
    customer_features
    .merge(cadence_features, on='CustomerID', how='left', validate='one_to_one')
    .merge(cancellation_features, on='CustomerID', how='left', validate='one_to_one')
)

Modeling, Profiling & Holdout Roles¶

  • Eleven modeling candidates and eight profiling fields registered explicitly (Table 7)
  • Country and calendar dates are retained to explain and audit segments, not to create them
  • Recording the role of each field in advance keeps holdout outcomes out of the clustering inputs by construction

Feature Table Validation¶

  • Structural gate run before any chart or model: uniqueness, completeness, sign constraints, and the absence of holdout fields among modeling candidates (Table 8)
  • All eight checks passed, so any later problem is a modeling issue rather than a data-construction issue
In [9]:
# Customer Table Validation
validation_checks = {

    'No missing customer identifiers': customer_features['CustomerID'].notna().all(),
    'At least one positive order': customer_features['order_count'].ge(1).all(),
    'Positive development revenue': customer_features['total_revenue'].gt(0).all(),

Coverage & Distribution Shape¶

  • No missing values across any of the eleven modeling candidates (Table 9)
  • Severe right skew on the monetary and volume measures: total revenue 23.67, average units per order 50.10, order count 10.62
  • Recency and tenure are close to symmetric (0.77 and 0.45), so scale differences rather than shape dominate the raw matrix
  • Spearman correlations show the redundancy that motivates feature selection: order count, active days, and unique products move together, as do total revenue and its per-order components (Figure 1)
In [10]:
# Feature Coverage & Distribution Diagnostics
feature_diagnostics = pd.DataFrame({
    'Feature': modeling_candidates,

    'Median': [customer_features[field].median() for field in modeling_candidates],
    '95th percentile': [customer_features[field].quantile(0.95) for field in modeling_candidates],
    'Maximum': [customer_features[field].max() for field in modeling_candidates],

05Shared Modeling Matrix

  • Every clustering method received the same customer population, selected features, transformations, and scaling
  • Holding preprocessing constant isolates differences in clustering methodology from differences introduced by data preparation
  • Seven behaviors were retained, each representing a distinct business concept, so no single behavior influences distance several times over

Feature Selection¶

  • Selected: recency, order count, total revenue, average units per order, average products per order, tenure, and cancellation rate (Table 10)
  • Active days dropped because order count already represents purchase frequency
  • Average and median order value dropped because total revenue and order count already encode their components
  • Unique products dropped because it grows mechanically with activity; products per order gives a comparable measure of basket breadth
  • The four excluded candidates remain available for profiling

Preprocessing¶

  • Three transparent steps, fixed before any method was fit (Table 11)
  • Extreme influence limited by capping each feature at its 1st and 99th percentiles, without removing customers
  • Right skew reduced with log1p on the six nonnegative count and value measures; cancellation rate stays on its original zero-to-one scale
  • Comparable scales created with robust scaling: median subtracted, interquartile range divided out
  • Original customer measures were left unchanged for segment interpretation
In [13]:
# Preprocessing Pipeline: Cap, Log, Robust Scale
LOWER_QUANTILE = 0.01
UPPER_QUANTILE = 0.99
LOG_FEATURES = [feature for feature in FINAL_FEATURES if feature != 'cancellation_rate']

X_raw = (
    customer_features
    .set_index('CustomerID')[FINAL_FEATURES]
    .astype(float)
)

winsor_bounds = pd.DataFrame({
    'lower_bound': X_raw.quantile(LOWER_QUANTILE),
    'upper_bound': X_raw.quantile(UPPER_QUANTILE),
})

X_capped = X_raw.copy()
for feature in FINAL_FEATURES:
    X_capped[feature] = X_capped[feature].clip(
        lower=winsor_bounds.loc[feature, 'lower_bound'],
        upper=winsor_bounds.loc[feature, 'upper_bound'],
    )

X_transformed = X_capped.copy()
X_transformed[LOG_FEATURES] = np.log1p(X_transformed[LOG_FEATURES])

scaler = RobustScaler(quantile_range=(25, 75))
X_scaled = pd.DataFrame(
    scaler.fit_transform(X_transformed),
    index=X_transformed.index,
    columns=FINAL_FEATURES,
)

preprocessing_summary = (
    winsor_bounds
    .rename_axis('Feature')
    .reset_index()
    .assign(
        Transformation=lambda frame: frame['Feature'].map(
            lambda feature: 'Cap, log1p, robust scale'
            if feature in LOG_FEATURES
            else 'Cap, robust scale'
        )
    )
)

display(
    preprocessing_summary.style
    .hide(axis='index')
    .format({'lower_bound': '{:,.3f}', 'upper_bound': '{:,.3f}'})
    .set_properties(subset=['Feature', 'Transformation'], **{'text-align': 'left'})
    .set_properties(subset=['lower_bound', 'upper_bound'], **{'text-align': 'right'})
    .set_table_styles([{'selector': 'th', 'props': [('text-align', 'left')]}])
)

Effect of Transformation¶

  • Skew reduction is substantial where it mattered: average units per order 50.10 to -0.69, total revenue 23.67 to 0.22, order count 10.62 to 0.89 (Table 12)
  • Recency and tenure shifted slightly negative, an expected consequence of applying log1p to already-symmetric measures
  • After scaling, all seven features occupy a comparable range centered on zero, with no feature able to dominate distance through scale alone (Figure 2)
  • This is a preprocessing diagnostic; it is not evidence that clusters exist

Matrix Validation¶

  • Seven checks confirmed the matrix preserved the customer population and produced complete, finite, consistently scaled values (Table 13)
  • All passed: 4,966 customers by 7 features, identifiers intact, no missing or infinite values, every feature varying, medians centered at zero

06Candidate Segmentation Methods

  • Built the full set of candidate segmentations without selecting a winner, keeping algorithm choice and configuration choice as separate decisions
  • RFM rules provide the practical business baseline: simple to explain, simple to refresh, and directly applicable to new customers
  • Six clustering families then test different assumptions about customer structure using the same shared matrix: centroid (K-means), probabilistic (Gaussian mixture), hierarchical (Ward), density (DBSCAN, HDBSCAN), and graph-based (spectral)
  • A clustering method had to deliver material incremental value to justify its greater complexity

RFM Business Baseline¶

  • Recency, order frequency, and total revenue each binned into five value-based groups, with higher scores meaning more recent, more frequent, and more valuable
  • Customers holding the same value always receive the same score, so identical customers are never separated by row order
  • Frequency produced 4 groups rather than 5: 2,411 customers placed one or two orders, a tie mass larger than a quintile, so the lowest bins merge
  • The combined score was divided into five portfolio segments on the same basis, leaving them unequal in size, from 14.5% to 28.8% of customers (Table 15)
In [18]:
# RFM Business Baseline
RFM_SEGMENT_NAMES = {
    0: 'Lower activity',
    1: 'Developing',
    2: 'Core',
    3: 'High value',
    4: 'Top value',
}

rfm = customer_features.set_index('CustomerID')[
    ['recency_days', 'order_count', 'total_revenue']
].copy()

def quintile_score(values: pd.Series, ascending: bool = True) -> pd.Series:
    """Score customers into five value-based groups.

    Customers holding the same value always receive the same score. Repeated
    quantile edges are dropped, so a measure with heavy ties yields fewer than
    five groups instead of separating identical customers by row order.
    """
    ordered = values if ascending else -values
    return pd.qcut(ordered, q=5, labels=False, duplicates='drop').astype(int) + 1

rfm['recency_score'] = quintile_score(rfm['recency_days'], ascending=False)
rfm['frequency_score'] = quintile_score(rfm['order_count'])
rfm['monetary_score'] = quintile_score(rfm['total_revenue'])
rfm['rfm_total'] = rfm[
    ['recency_score', 'frequency_score', 'monetary_score']
].sum(axis=1)
rfm['rfm_segment'] = quintile_score(rfm['rfm_total']) - 1
rfm['rfm_segment_name'] = rfm['rfm_segment'].map(RFM_SEGMENT_NAMES)

if rfm['rfm_segment_name'].isna().any():
    raise ValueError('Segment naming requires one label for each observed RFM group.')

print(
    'Groups produced after tie-preserving binning: '
    f"recency {rfm['recency_score'].nunique()}, "
    f"frequency {rfm['frequency_score'].nunique()}, "
    f"monetary {rfm['monetary_score'].nunique()}, "
    f"portfolio segments {rfm['rfm_segment'].nunique()}"
)

rfm_summary = (
    rfm.groupby(['rfm_segment', 'rfm_segment_name'], as_index=False)
    .agg(
        customers=('rfm_total', 'size'),
        median_recency=('recency_days', 'median'),
        median_orders=('order_count', 'median'),
        median_revenue=('total_revenue', 'median'),
    )
)
rfm_summary['customer_share'] = rfm_summary['customers'] / len(rfm)

display(
    rfm_summary.style
    .hide(axis='index')
    .format({
        'customers': '{:,.0f}',
        'customer_share': '{:.1%}',
        'median_recency': '{:,.0f}',
        'median_orders': '{:,.1f}',
        'median_revenue': '£{:,.0f}',
    })
    .bar(subset=['customer_share'], color='#9ecae1', vmin=0, vmax=1)
    .set_properties(subset=['rfm_segment_name'], **{'text-align': 'left'})
    .set_properties(
        subset=['rfm_segment', 'customers', 'customer_share', 'median_recency', 'median_orders', 'median_revenue'],
        **{'text-align': 'right'},
    )
    .set_table_styles([{'selector': 'th', 'props': [('text-align', 'left')]}])
)

Candidate Registry¶

  • Each solution was stored with its labels, parameters, runtime, retained cluster count, noise share, and cluster-size range
  • Recording every fitted configuration keeps feasibility description separate from ranking
  • Noise from density methods is kept as label -1 and treated as a real operational population rather than discarded
In [19]:
# Candidate Registration Function
candidate_labels = {}
candidate_records = []

def register_candidate(
    solution_id,
    family,
    method,
    labels,
    parameters,
    runtime_seconds,
    status='Fitted',
):
    labels = np.asarray(labels, dtype=int)
    if len(labels) != len(X_scaled):
        raise ValueError(f'{solution_id} returned an unexpected label count.')

    retained = labels[labels != -1]
    cluster_sizes = pd.Series(retained).value_counts()
    noise_share = np.mean(labels == -1)

    candidate_labels[solution_id] = pd.Series(
        labels,
        index=X_scaled.index,
        name='cluster',
    )
    candidate_records.append({
        'solution_id': solution_id,
        'family': family,
        'method': method,
        'parameters': json.dumps(parameters, sort_keys=True),
        'status': status,
        'runtime_seconds': runtime_seconds,
        'cluster_count': cluster_sizes.size,
        'noise_share': noise_share,
        'smallest_cluster_share': (cluster_sizes.min() / len(labels)) if len(cluster_sizes) else np.nan,
        'largest_cluster_share': (cluster_sizes.max() / len(labels)) if len(cluster_sizes) else np.nan,
    })

register_candidate(
    solution_id='rfm_rules__five_groups',
    family='Business baseline',
    method='RFM rules',
    labels=rfm.loc[X_scaled.index, 'rfm_segment'].to_numpy(),
    parameters={'groups': 5, 'scoring': 'value-based quintiles'},
    runtime_seconds=0.0,
)

Fixed-Cluster Methods¶

  • K-means, Gaussian mixture, Ward, and spectral clustering each evaluated across the same two-through-ten cluster range
  • Evaluating identical configuration breadth avoids assuming the preferred number of customer groups in advance
In [20]:
# Fit K-Means, Gaussian Mixture & Ward Clustering
for k in K_RANGE:
    start = perf_counter()
    model = KMeans(
        n_clusters=k,
        n_init=20,
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    labels = model.fit_predict(X_scaled)
    register_candidate(
        solution_id=f'kmeans__k_{k}',
        family='Centroid',
        method='K-means',
        labels=labels,
        parameters={'n_clusters': k, 'n_init': 20},
        runtime_seconds=perf_counter() - start,
    )

for k in K_RANGE:
    start = perf_counter()
    model = GaussianMixture(
        n_components=k,
        covariance_type='full',
        n_init=5,
        reg_covar=1e-6,
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    labels = model.fit_predict(X_scaled)
    register_candidate(
        solution_id=f'gmm__k_{k}',
        family='Probabilistic',
        method='Gaussian mixture',
        labels=labels,
        parameters={
            'n_components': k,
            'covariance_type': 'full',
            'n_init': 5,
        },
        runtime_seconds=perf_counter() - start,
        status='Fitted' if model.converged_ else 'Convergence review',
    )

for k in K_RANGE:
    start = perf_counter()
    model = AgglomerativeClustering(
        n_clusters=k,
        linkage='ward',
    )
    labels = model.fit_predict(X_scaled)
    register_candidate(
        solution_id=f'ward__k_{k}',
        family='Hierarchical',
        method='Ward clustering',
        labels=labels,
        parameters={'n_clusters': k, 'linkage': 'ward'},
        runtime_seconds=perf_counter() - start,
    )

Density-Based Methods¶

  • DBSCAN distance thresholds derived from the observed nearest-neighbor distance distribution, at the 80th, 90th, and 95th percentiles for each of three minimum-neighbor settings
  • HDBSCAN evaluated three minimum cluster sizes (25, 50, 100) against two neighborhood requirements (10, 20)
  • Neither method requires a fixed cluster count, and both may assign customers to noise
In [21]:
# Fit DBSCAN
DBSCAN_MIN_SAMPLES = [10, 20, 30]
DBSCAN_DISTANCE_QUANTILES = [0.80, 0.90, 0.95]

for min_samples in DBSCAN_MIN_SAMPLES:
    neighbor_model = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=min_samples)
    neighbor_distances = neighbor_model.fit(X_scaled).kneighbors()[0][:, -1]

    for distance_quantile in DBSCAN_DISTANCE_QUANTILES:
        eps = float(np.quantile(neighbor_distances, distance_quantile))
        start = perf_counter()
        model = DBSCAN(
            eps=eps,
            min_samples=min_samples,
            metric='euclidean',
            n_jobs=-1,
        )
        labels = model.fit_predict(X_scaled)
        register_candidate(
            solution_id=(
                f'dbscan__min_{min_samples}'
                f'__q_{int(distance_quantile * 100)}'
            ),
            family='Density',
            method='DBSCAN',
            labels=labels,
            parameters={
                'eps': round(eps, 6),
                'min_samples': min_samples,
                'distance_quantile': distance_quantile,
            },
            runtime_seconds=perf_counter() - start,
        )
In [22]:
# Fit HDBSCAN
try:
    from sklearn.cluster import HDBSCAN
    HDBSCAN_SOURCE = 'scikit-learn'
except ImportError:
    try:
        from hdbscan import HDBSCAN
        HDBSCAN_SOURCE = 'hdbscan package'
    except ImportError:
        HDBSCAN = None
        HDBSCAN_SOURCE = None

HDBSCAN_MIN_CLUSTER_SIZES = [25, 50, 100]
HDBSCAN_MIN_SAMPLES = [10, 20]

if HDBSCAN is None:
    raise ImportError(
        'HDBSCAN is unavailable. Install a recent scikit-learn release '        'or the hdbscan package before continuing.'
    )

for min_cluster_size in HDBSCAN_MIN_CLUSTER_SIZES:
    for min_samples in HDBSCAN_MIN_SAMPLES:
        start = perf_counter()
        model = HDBSCAN(
            min_cluster_size=min_cluster_size,
            min_samples=min_samples,
            metric='euclidean',
        )
        labels = model.fit_predict(X_scaled)
        register_candidate(
            solution_id=(
                f'hdbscan__size_{min_cluster_size}'
                f'__min_{min_samples}'
            ),
            family='Density',
            method='HDBSCAN',
            labels=labels,
            parameters={
                'min_cluster_size': min_cluster_size,
                'min_samples': min_samples,
                'implementation': HDBSCAN_SOURCE,
            },
            runtime_seconds=perf_counter() - start,
        )

Graph-Based Method¶

  • Spectral clustering built on a 15-nearest-neighbor graph across the same two-through-ten cluster range
  • Runtime was retained as part of the later operational assessment, since refresh cost is relevant to deployment
In [23]:
# Fit Spectral Clustering
SPECTRAL_NEIGHBORS = min(15, len(X_scaled) - 1)

for k in K_RANGE:
    start = perf_counter()
    model = SpectralClustering(
        n_clusters=k,
        affinity='nearest_neighbors',
        n_neighbors=SPECTRAL_NEIGHBORS,
        assign_labels='kmeans',
        n_init=10,
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
        n_jobs=-1,
    )
    labels = model.fit_predict(X_scaled)
    register_candidate(
        solution_id=f'spectral__k_{k}',
        family='Graph',
        method='Spectral clustering',
        labels=labels,
        parameters={
            'n_clusters': k,
            'affinity': 'nearest_neighbors',
            'n_neighbors': SPECTRAL_NEIGHBORS,
        },
        runtime_seconds=perf_counter() - start,
    )

Candidate Inventory¶

  • 52 configurations fitted across all seven methods (Table 16)
  • DBSCAN and HDBSCAN are flagged on every configuration: DBSCAN produced between one and two clusters, HDBSCAN between 55.1% and 64.0% noise
  • Spectral clustering flagged on 5 of 9 configurations for producing a cluster below 1% of customers; Gaussian mixture on 2 of 9
  • K-means and Ward produced no initial feasibility concern at any cluster count
  • Five structural checks confirmed every method is represented, every solution has stored labels aligned to the matrix, and identifiers are unique (Table 17)

07Statistical Evidence

  • Asked two questions: do the groups form distinguishable structures, and do those structures persist when the customer sample changes
  • Silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz, cluster balance, noise share, and repeated-sample stability were retained as separate evidence rather than combined into one score
  • Statistical results can identify weak or fragile configurations; they cannot establish business usefulness

Internal Structure¶

  • Higher silhouette and Calinski-Harabasz indicate stronger separation; lower Davies-Bouldin indicates better separation
  • Density-method noise is excluded from the three indices but stays visible through the separate noise-share measure
  • Normalized cluster entropy was added as a balance measure, so a solution that hides a dominant cluster is visible
In [26]:
# Internal Structure Metrics
INTERNAL_METRIC_SAMPLE = min(3000, len(X_scaled))

def calculate_internal_metrics(labels):
    labels = np.asarray(labels, dtype=int)
    retained_mask = labels != -1
    retained_labels = labels[retained_mask]
    retained_matrix = X_scaled.to_numpy()[retained_mask]
    unique_labels = np.unique(retained_labels)

    if len(unique_labels) < 2 or len(retained_labels) <= len(unique_labels):
        return {
            'silhouette': np.nan,
            'davies_bouldin': np.nan,
            'calinski_harabasz': np.nan,
            'normalized_cluster_entropy': np.nan,
        }

    cluster_shares = pd.Series(retained_labels).value_counts(normalize=True)
    entropy = -(cluster_shares * np.log(cluster_shares)).sum()
    normalized_entropy = entropy / np.log(len(cluster_shares))

    return {
        'silhouette': silhouette_score(
            retained_matrix,
            retained_labels,
            sample_size=min(INTERNAL_METRIC_SAMPLE, len(retained_labels)),
            random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
        ),
        'davies_bouldin': davies_bouldin_score(retained_matrix, retained_labels),
        'calinski_harabasz': calinski_harabasz_score(retained_matrix, retained_labels),
        'normalized_cluster_entropy': normalized_entropy,
    }

internal_records = []
for solution_id, labels in candidate_labels.items():
    internal_records.append({
        'solution_id': solution_id,
        **calculate_internal_metrics(labels.to_numpy()),
    })

internal_results = pd.DataFrame(internal_records)

Repeated-Sample Stability¶

  • Each configuration was refitted five times on common 2,000-customer samples and compared with the original labels for those same customers, using adjusted Rand index
  • A stable solution should reproduce similar groupings when a reasonable portion of the customer population changes
  • Density parameters were held at their absolute values during refitting, which penalizes DBSCAN and HDBSCAN on a smaller sample; the comparison is therefore conservative toward the density families
In [27]:
# Stability Samples & Refit Functions
N_STABILITY_RUNS = 5
STABILITY_SAMPLE_SIZE = min(2000, len(X_scaled))
stability_rng = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_STATE)

stability_samples = [
    pd.Index(
        stability_rng.choice(
            X_scaled.index.to_numpy(),
            size=STABILITY_SAMPLE_SIZE,
            replace=False,
        )
    )
    for _ in range(N_STABILITY_RUNS)
]

def build_sample_rfm_labels(customer_ids):
    sample = rfm.loc[customer_ids, ['recency_days', 'order_count', 'total_revenue']].copy()
    sample['r'] = quintile_score(sample['recency_days'], ascending=False)
    sample['f'] = quintile_score(sample['order_count'])
    sample['m'] = quintile_score(sample['total_revenue'])
    sample['total'] = sample[['r', 'f', 'm']].sum(axis=1)
    return (quintile_score(sample['total']) - 1).to_numpy()

def refit_candidate(method, parameters, customer_ids):
    sample_matrix = X_scaled.loc[customer_ids]

    if method == 'RFM rules':
        return build_sample_rfm_labels(customer_ids)
    if method == 'K-means':
        model = KMeans(
            n_clusters=parameters['n_clusters'],
            n_init=parameters['n_init'],
            random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
        )
    elif method == 'Gaussian mixture':
        model = GaussianMixture(
            n_components=parameters['n_components'],
            covariance_type=parameters['covariance_type'],
            n_init=parameters['n_init'],
            reg_covar=1e-6,
            random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
        )
    elif method == 'Ward clustering':
        model = AgglomerativeClustering(
            n_clusters=parameters['n_clusters'],
            linkage=parameters['linkage'],
        )
    elif method == 'DBSCAN':
        model = DBSCAN(
            eps=parameters['eps'],
            min_samples=parameters['min_samples'],
            metric='euclidean',
            n_jobs=-1,
        )
    elif method == 'HDBSCAN':
        model = HDBSCAN(
            min_cluster_size=parameters['min_cluster_size'],
            min_samples=parameters['min_samples'],
            metric='euclidean',
        )
    elif method == 'Spectral clustering':
        model = SpectralClustering(
            n_clusters=parameters['n_clusters'],
            affinity=parameters['affinity'],
            n_neighbors=min(parameters['n_neighbors'], len(sample_matrix) - 1),
            assign_labels='kmeans',
            n_init=10,
            random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
            n_jobs=-1,
        )
    else:
        raise ValueError(f'Unsupported method: {method}')

    return model.fit_predict(sample_matrix)
In [28]:
# Repeated-Sample Stability Runs
stability_records = []

for row in candidate_inventory.itertuples(index=False):
    parameters = json.loads(row.parameters)
    reference_labels = candidate_labels[row.solution_id]

    for run_number, customer_ids in enumerate(stability_samples, start=1):
        start = perf_counter()
        sample_labels = refit_candidate(row.method, parameters, customer_ids)
        reference_sample = reference_labels.loc[customer_ids].to_numpy()
        stability_records.append({
            'solution_id': row.solution_id,
            'run': run_number,
            'adjusted_rand_index': adjusted_rand_score(
                reference_sample, sample_labels
            ),
            'runtime_seconds': perf_counter() - start,
        })

stability_runs = pd.DataFrame(stability_records)
stability_results = (
    stability_runs.groupby('solution_id', as_index=False)
    .agg(
        stability_mean=('adjusted_rand_index', 'mean'),
        stability_sd=('adjusted_rand_index', 'std'),
        stability_10th=('adjusted_rand_index', lambda values: values.quantile(0.10)),
        stability_90th=('adjusted_rand_index', lambda values: values.quantile(0.90)),
        stability_minimum=('adjusted_rand_index', 'min'),
        stability_runtime_seconds=('runtime_seconds', 'sum'),
    )
)

Statistical Review Gates¶

  • A configuration proceeds without an initial concern when it produces at least two groups, assigns no more than 50% of customers to noise, keeps every cluster above 1% of customers, fits successfully, and reaches mean stability of at least 0.70
  • These are study conventions for screening commercially implausible or fragile solutions, not universal clustering standards
In [29]:
# Statistical Review Gates
MINIMUM_STABILITY = 0.70
MAXIMUM_NOISE_SHARE = 0.50
MINIMUM_CLUSTER_SHARE = 0.01

statistical_results = (
    candidate_inventory
    .merge(internal_results, on='solution_id', how='left', validate='one_to_one')
    .merge(stability_results, on='solution_id', how='left', validate='one_to_one')
)

def statistical_review_reason(row):
    reasons = []
    if row['cluster_count'] < 2:
        reasons.append('fewer than two clusters')
    if row['noise_share'] > MAXIMUM_NOISE_SHARE:
        reasons.append('noise above 50%')
    if row['smallest_cluster_share'] < MINIMUM_CLUSTER_SHARE:
        reasons.append('cluster below 1%')
    if row['status'] != 'Fitted':
        reasons.append('fit status')
    if row['stability_mean'] < MINIMUM_STABILITY:
        reasons.append('stability below 0.70')
    return 'No initial concern' if not reasons else '; '.join(reasons)

statistical_results['statistical_review'] = statistical_results.apply(
    statistical_review_reason, axis=1
)
statistical_results['passes_initial_gates'] = (
    statistical_results['statistical_review'].eq('No initial concern')
)

Evidence by Method¶

  • 16 of 52 configurations proceeded without an initial statistical concern (Table 18)
  • Ward clustering failed the stability gate at every cluster count, peaking at 0.476: the hierarchical structure did not reproduce on resampled customers
  • DBSCAN posted the highest silhouette of any method (0.482), but on one-and-two-cluster solutions that carry no business meaning, a reminder that internal indices reward degenerate structure
  • K-means and Gaussian mixture both reached 0.940 stability; spectral clustering reached 0.931
  • The RFM baseline reached 0.889 stability with a low silhouette (0.055), expected for rules that cut a continuous space rather than follow its geometry
  • Silhouette generally declines as cluster count rises, while stability is strongest at small cluster counts and degrades unevenly beyond six groups (Figure 3)
  • Every density configuration sits below the stability threshold, and the HDBSCAN solutions sit far to the right of the noise limit (Figure 4)

08Business Evidence

  • Asked whether statistically credible segmentations also separate customers in ways that matter commercially
  • Development-period profiles describe the groups that were discovered; the later six months test whether those groups still differentiate activity, orders, revenue, and product breadth
  • Holdout results describe out-of-time behavioral differentiation, not evidence that segment membership causes future behavior

Holdout Outcomes¶

  • Every development customer stays in the evaluation population; those without a valid holdout purchase receive zero activity, orders, revenue, units, and breadth rather than disappearing (Table 20)
  • 2,581 of 4,966 development customers (52.0%) purchased again in the holdout window
  • Holdout activity totals 8,812 orders and £4,625,733 in revenue
In [34]:
# Customer-Level Holdout Outcomes
holdout = transactions.loc[transactions['study_period'].eq('Holdout')].copy()
holdout['has_customer_id'] = holdout['CustomerID'].notna()

    holdout['has_customer_id']
    & holdout['InvoiceDate'].notna()
    & ~holdout['is_cancellation']
    & holdout['Quantity'].gt(0)

)

Outcome Differentiation¶

  • For each solution, the share of customer-level outcome variation associated with segment assignment (η²) was measured separately for development revenue, holdout activity, holdout orders, holdout revenue, and holdout product breadth
  • Keeping the measures separate prevents strong differentiation on one outcome from concealing weak differentiation on another
  • η² rises mechanically with the number of groups, so values are not comparable across solutions of different size without the cluster-count trade-off applied later
In [35]:
# Outcome Differentiation & Segment Profiles
BUSINESS_OUTCOME_FIELDS = [
    'development_revenue',
    'holdout_active',
    'holdout_orders',
    'holdout_revenue',
    'holdout_unique_skus',
]

def variance_explained_by_groups(labels, values):
    labels = np.asarray(labels)
    values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    valid = np.isfinite(values)
    labels = labels[valid]
    values = values[valid]

    if len(values) == 0:
        return np.nan
    grand_mean = values.mean()
    total_ss = np.square(values - grand_mean).sum()
    if total_ss == 0:
        return 0.0

    between_ss = 0.0
    for group in np.unique(labels):
        group_values = values[labels == group]
        between_ss += len(group_values) * np.square(group_values.mean() - grand_mean)
    return between_ss / total_ss

business_score_records = []
segment_profile_frames = []

for solution_id in statistically_eligible_ids:
    labels = candidate_labels[solution_id].loc[business_outcomes.index]
    evaluation = business_outcomes.copy()
    evaluation['cluster'] = labels.to_numpy()

    profile = (
        evaluation.groupby('cluster', as_index=False)
        .agg(
            customers=('development_revenue', 'size'),
            development_revenue=('development_revenue', 'sum'),
            median_development_revenue=('development_revenue', 'median'),
            median_development_orders=('development_orders', 'median'),
            median_recency=('recency_days', 'median'),
            holdout_active_rate=('holdout_active', 'mean'),
            holdout_revenue=('holdout_revenue', 'sum'),
            holdout_revenue_per_customer=('holdout_revenue', 'mean'),
            holdout_orders_per_customer=('holdout_orders', 'mean'),
            holdout_skus_per_customer=('holdout_unique_skus', 'mean'),
        )
    )
    profile['customer_share'] = profile['customers'] / profile['customers'].sum()
    profile['development_revenue_share'] = (
        profile['development_revenue'] / profile['development_revenue'].sum()
    )
    profile['holdout_revenue_share'] = (
        profile['holdout_revenue'] / profile['holdout_revenue'].sum()
    )
    profile['holdout_revenue_lift'] = (
        profile['holdout_revenue_share'] / profile['customer_share']
    )
    profile.insert(0, 'solution_id', solution_id)
    segment_profile_frames.append(profile)

    record = {'solution_id': solution_id}
    for field in BUSINESS_OUTCOME_FIELDS:
        record[f'{field}_eta2'] = variance_explained_by_groups(
            labels.to_numpy(), business_outcomes[field].to_numpy()
        )
    record['holdout_activity_spread'] = (
        profile['holdout_active_rate'].max() - profile['holdout_active_rate'].min()
    )
    record['maximum_holdout_revenue_lift'] = profile['holdout_revenue_lift'].max()
    business_score_records.append(record)

segment_profiles = pd.concat(segment_profile_frames, ignore_index=True)
business_scores = pd.DataFrame(business_score_records)

Customer-Sampling Uncertainty¶

  • 200 common customer-level bootstrap samples estimate uncertainty around holdout activity and revenue differentiation
  • Every candidate was evaluated on the same resampled customer positions, so small point-estimate differences are not treated as decisive
  • Segment labels are held fixed during resampling, so the intervals capture customer-sampling variation only, not variation from re-estimating the segments
In [36]:
# Customer-Sampling Bootstrap Intervals
N_BUSINESS_BOOTSTRAPS = 200
business_rng = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_STATE + 1)
bootstrap_positions = [
    business_rng.integers(0, len(business_outcomes), size=len(business_outcomes))
    for _ in range(N_BUSINESS_BOOTSTRAPS)
]

holdout_revenue_values = business_outcomes['holdout_revenue'].to_numpy()
holdout_activity_values = business_outcomes['holdout_active'].to_numpy()
business_bootstrap_records = []

for solution_id in statistically_eligible_ids:
    labels = candidate_labels[solution_id].loc[business_outcomes.index].to_numpy()
    for iteration, positions in enumerate(bootstrap_positions, start=1):
        sampled_labels = labels[positions]
        business_bootstrap_records.append({
            'solution_id': solution_id,
            'iteration': iteration,
            'holdout_revenue_eta2': variance_explained_by_groups(
                sampled_labels, holdout_revenue_values[positions]
            ),
            'holdout_activity_eta2': variance_explained_by_groups(
                sampled_labels, holdout_activity_values[positions]
            ),
        })

business_bootstrap = pd.DataFrame(business_bootstrap_records)
business_intervals = (
    business_bootstrap.groupby('solution_id', as_index=False)
    .agg(
        holdout_revenue_eta2_p05=('holdout_revenue_eta2', lambda values: values.quantile(0.05)),
        holdout_revenue_eta2_median=('holdout_revenue_eta2', 'median'),
        holdout_revenue_eta2_p95=('holdout_revenue_eta2', lambda values: values.quantile(0.95)),
        holdout_activity_eta2_p05=('holdout_activity_eta2', lambda values: values.quantile(0.05)),
        holdout_activity_eta2_median=('holdout_activity_eta2', 'median'),
        holdout_activity_eta2_p95=('holdout_activity_eta2', lambda values: values.quantile(0.95)),
    )
)

Business Scorecard¶

  • The scorecard deliberately omits an overall weighted score, so consistent performers stay visibly different from solutions strong on one outcome only (Table 21)
  • RFM rules lead out-of-time differentiation on every holdout measure: activity 0.262, orders 0.223, product breadth 0.204, and development revenue 0.095
  • Gaussian mixture at four components edges RFM on holdout revenue alone (0.062 against 0.058)
  • The best K-means configuration reaches 0.203 activity and 0.048 revenue, below the baseline on both
  • Bootstrap intervals overlap heavily across the shortlist, confirming that point-estimate gaps of a few thousandths carry little information (Figure 5)

09Operational Fit

  • Tested whether the remaining solutions can be explained, refreshed, and applied to new customers
  • Quantitative checks measure segment contrast and geometric assignment margins; a separate register records assignment capability, noise handling, and refresh cost
  • Operational characteristics stay categorical, and no arbitrary weighted score was created

Segment Contrast & Assignment Margins¶

  • Feature contrast is the range of cluster medians on the shared scaled matrix; a feature has material contrast when that range reaches one scaled unit (Table 24)
  • K-means at four through six clusters separates all seven features; RFM separates four; Gaussian mixture at two clusters and K-means at two clusters separate none
  • Assignment margin compares each customer's distance to its own centroid against the nearest alternative
  • RFM records the lowest median margin on the shortlist (0.069), the expected cost of rules that cut a continuous space rather than follow its geometry
  • Gaussian mixture and spectral solutions carry negative 10th-percentile margins, meaning a tenth of their customers sit closer to another segment's centroid than to their own
  • The reference heatmap shows the RFM signature: recency falling and revenue, frequency, and basket breadth rising monotonically across segments (Figure 6)
In [41]:
# Segment Contrast & Assignment Margins
MATERIAL_CONTRAST_THRESHOLD = 1.0

def assignment_margin_summary(labels):
    labels = np.asarray(labels)
    retained = labels != -1
    retained_matrix = X_scaled.to_numpy()[retained]
    retained_labels = labels[retained]
    groups = np.unique(retained_labels)

    if len(groups) < 2 or len(retained_matrix) == 0:
        return np.nan, np.nan

    centroids = np.vstack([
        retained_matrix[retained_labels == group].mean(axis=0)
        for group in groups
    ])
    distances = np.sqrt(
        np.square(retained_matrix[:, None, :] - centroids[None, :, :]).sum(axis=2)
    )
    group_to_column = {group: position for position, group in enumerate(groups)}
    own_columns = np.array([group_to_column[group] for group in retained_labels])
    row_positions = np.arange(len(retained_matrix))
    own_distance = distances[row_positions, own_columns]
    alternative_distances = distances.copy()
    alternative_distances[row_positions, own_columns] = np.inf
    nearest_alternative = alternative_distances.min(axis=1)
    margins = (nearest_alternative - own_distance) / (nearest_alternative + 1e-12)
    return float(np.median(margins)), float(np.quantile(margins, 0.10))

interpretability_records = []
scaled_segment_profiles = {}

for solution_id in business_results['solution_id']:
    labels = candidate_labels[solution_id].loc[X_scaled.index]
    profile = (
        X_scaled.assign(cluster=labels.to_numpy())
        .loc[lambda frame: frame['cluster'].ne(-1)]
        .groupby('cluster')[FINAL_FEATURES]
        .median()
    )
    scaled_segment_profiles[solution_id] = profile
    feature_contrast = profile.max(axis=0) - profile.min(axis=0)
    median_margin, tenth_percentile_margin = assignment_margin_summary(labels)

    interpretability_records.append({
        'solution_id': solution_id,
        'features_with_material_contrast': int(
            feature_contrast.ge(MATERIAL_CONTRAST_THRESHOLD).sum()
        ),
        'maximum_feature_contrast': float(feature_contrast.max()),
        'minimum_cluster_signature': float(profile.abs().max(axis=1).min()),
        'median_assignment_margin': median_margin,
        'assignment_margin_p10': tenth_percentile_margin,
    })

interpretability_results = pd.DataFrame(interpretability_records)

    })
)

Operating Model¶

  • The register describes method capabilities rather than scoring them (Table 25)
  • Native assignment: RFM rules, K-means, and Gaussian mixture can classify a new customer directly
  • No native assignment: Ward, DBSCAN, and spectral clustering require a documented surrogate model or a refit
  • Refresh effort is lowest for RFM rules and K-means, highest for spectral clustering

Trade-off Matrix & Pareto Shortlist¶

  • A candidate is Pareto-efficient when no other candidate is at least as good on every included measure and strictly better on at least one (Table 26)
  • The comparison rewards stability, holdout differentiation, assignment margin, and minimum segment size, while penalizing noise, segment count, and evaluation runtime
  • Seven candidates are efficient: RFM rules, K-means at two through six clusters, and Gaussian mixture at four components
  • RFM rules sit at the top-right of the stability and revenue-differentiation frontier while retaining a low-effort refresh path (Figure 7)
In [44]:
# Trade-off Matrix & Pareto Shortlist
decision_matrix = (
    business_results
    .merge(interpretability_results, on='solution_id', how='left', validate='one_to_one')
    .merge(operational_register, on='method', how='left', validate='many_to_one')
)
decision_matrix['evaluation_runtime_seconds'] = (
    decision_matrix['runtime_seconds'] + decision_matrix['stability_runtime_seconds']
)

PARETO_MAXIMIZE = [
    'stability_mean', 'holdout_revenue_eta2', 'holdout_active_eta2',
    'median_assignment_margin', 'smallest_cluster_share',
]
PARETO_MINIMIZE = ['noise_share', 'cluster_count', 'evaluation_runtime_seconds']

def identify_pareto_efficient(frame, maximize, minimize, tolerance=1e-12):
    maximize_values = frame[maximize].fillna(-np.inf).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    minimize_values = frame[minimize].fillna(np.inf).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    efficient = np.ones(len(frame), dtype=bool)

    for candidate in range(len(frame)):
        for challenger in range(len(frame)):
            if candidate == challenger:
                continue
            no_worse = (
                np.all(maximize_values[challenger] >= maximize_values[candidate] - tolerance)
                and np.all(minimize_values[challenger] <= minimize_values[candidate] + tolerance)
            )
            strictly_better = (
                np.any(maximize_values[challenger] > maximize_values[candidate] + tolerance)
                or np.any(minimize_values[challenger] < minimize_values[candidate] - tolerance)
            )
            if no_worse and strictly_better:
                efficient[candidate] = False
                break
    return efficient

decision_matrix['pareto_efficient'] = identify_pareto_efficient(
    decision_matrix, PARETO_MAXIMIZE, PARETO_MINIMIZE
)
rfm_reference_ids = decision_matrix.loc[
    decision_matrix['method'].eq('RFM rules'), 'solution_id'
]
decision_candidate_ids = set(
    decision_matrix.loc[decision_matrix['pareto_efficient'], 'solution_id']
) | set(rfm_reference_ids)
decision_candidates = decision_matrix.loc[
    decision_matrix['solution_id'].isin(decision_candidate_ids)
].copy()

decision_display_columns = [
    'method', 'solution_id', 'cluster_count', 'noise_share', 'stability_mean',

10Sensitivity Analysis

  • Tested the Pareto candidates and the RFM and K-means baselines under reasonable preprocessing changes
  • Three alternatives: modestly tighter capping (2nd and 98th percentiles), a wider robust-scaling range (10th to 90th), and removal of the logarithmic transformation
  • Adjusted Rand index measures whether customer assignments remain similar to the primary specification; holdout outcomes were then re-evaluated without entering the clustering inputs

Preprocessing Scenarios¶

  • The clustering solutions do not survive the test (Table 28)
  • Worst-case assignment agreement with the primary specification: K-means at two clusters 0.007, K-means at four 0.075, K-means at three and five 0.158, K-means at six 0.168, Gaussian mixture at four 0.177
  • At those values the segments are effectively unrelated to the primary solution: the same customer receives a different assignment once a preprocessing choice changes
  • RFM rules score 1.000, structurally rather than empirically: capping, log1p, and robust scaling are all monotone, and the rules depend only on rank order, so they cannot move
  • Business differentiation degrades alongside assignment: Gaussian mixture falls from 0.062 to 0.022 on holdout revenue, while RFM holds at 0.058 and 0.262 (Figure 8)
  • Minimum segment size under the worst scenario also separates the field: RFM 14.5%, K-means at six clusters 1.6%
In [47]:
# Preprocessing Scenarios & Sensitivity Refits
kmeans_reference_ids = set(
    decision_matrix.loc[decision_matrix['method'].eq('K-means'), 'solution_id']
)
sensitivity_candidate_ids = set(decision_candidate_ids) | kmeans_reference_ids
sensitivity_candidates = decision_matrix.loc[
    decision_matrix['solution_id'].isin(sensitivity_candidate_ids)
].copy()

PREPROCESSING_SCENARIOS = {
    'Primary specification': {
        'lower_quantile': 0.01, 'upper_quantile': 0.99,
        'log_transform': True, 'scale_quantiles': (25, 75),
    },
    'Moderate capping': {
        'lower_quantile': 0.02, 'upper_quantile': 0.98,
        'log_transform': True, 'scale_quantiles': (25, 75),
    },
    'Wider robust scaling': {
        'lower_quantile': 0.01, 'upper_quantile': 0.99,
        'log_transform': True, 'scale_quantiles': (10, 90),
    },
    'No logarithmic transformation': {
        'lower_quantile': 0.01, 'upper_quantile': 0.99,
        'log_transform': False, 'scale_quantiles': (25, 75),
    },
}

def build_sensitivity_matrix(specification):
    matrix = X_raw.copy()
    lower = matrix.quantile(specification['lower_quantile'])
    upper = matrix.quantile(specification['upper_quantile'])
    for feature in FINAL_FEATURES:
        matrix[feature] = matrix[feature].clip(lower=lower[feature], upper=upper[feature])
    if specification['log_transform']:
        matrix[LOG_FEATURES] = np.log1p(matrix[LOG_FEATURES])
    scenario_scaler = RobustScaler(quantile_range=specification['scale_quantiles'])
    return pd.DataFrame(
        scenario_scaler.fit_transform(matrix),
        index=matrix.index, columns=matrix.columns,
    )

def refit_solution_for_sensitivity(solution_id, matrix):
    inventory_row = candidate_inventory.set_index('solution_id').loc[solution_id]
    method = inventory_row['method']
    parameters = json.loads(inventory_row['parameters'])

    if method == 'RFM rules':
        return rfm.loc[matrix.index, 'rfm_segment'].to_numpy()
    if method == 'K-means':
        return KMeans(
            n_clusters=parameters['n_clusters'], n_init=parameters['n_init'],
            random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
        ).fit_predict(matrix)
    if method == 'Gaussian mixture':
        return GaussianMixture(
            n_components=parameters['n_components'],
            covariance_type=parameters['covariance_type'],
            n_init=parameters['n_init'], reg_covar=1e-6, random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
        ).fit_predict(matrix)
    if method == 'Ward clustering':
        return AgglomerativeClustering(
            n_clusters=parameters['n_clusters'], linkage='ward',
        ).fit_predict(matrix)
    if method == 'DBSCAN':
        neighbor_distances = (
            NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=parameters['min_samples'])
            .fit(matrix).kneighbors()[0][:, -1]
        )
        scenario_eps = float(np.quantile(
            neighbor_distances, parameters['distance_quantile']
        ))
        return DBSCAN(
            eps=scenario_eps, min_samples=parameters['min_samples'], n_jobs=-1,
        ).fit_predict(matrix)
    if method == 'HDBSCAN':
        return HDBSCAN(
            min_cluster_size=parameters['min_cluster_size'],
            min_samples=parameters['min_samples'], metric='euclidean',
        ).fit_predict(matrix)
    if method == 'Spectral clustering':
        return SpectralClustering(
            n_clusters=parameters['n_clusters'], affinity='nearest_neighbors',
            n_neighbors=parameters['n_neighbors'], assign_labels='kmeans',
            n_init=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1,
        ).fit_predict(matrix)
    raise ValueError(f'Unsupported method: {method}')

sensitivity_records = []

for scenario_name, specification in PREPROCESSING_SCENARIOS.items():
    scenario_matrix = build_sensitivity_matrix(specification)
    for solution_id in sorted(sensitivity_candidate_ids):
        start = perf_counter()
        scenario_labels = refit_solution_for_sensitivity(solution_id, scenario_matrix)
        elapsed = perf_counter() - start

Business-Tolerance Scenarios¶

  • The decision rule favors the simplest deployable solution that stays close to the strongest observed holdout evidence, using worst-case values across all four preprocessing specifications
  • A candidate must be near the best result on revenue or activity and retain a stated share of the best result on the other outcome
  • Strict (5% / 90%), balanced (10% / 80%), and broad (20% / 70%) settings show whether the recommendation depends on leadership's tolerance for trading differentiation against simplicity
  • RFM rules are the only sufficient candidate under all three settings (Table 29)
  • The result is insensitive to tolerance because the gap is not marginal: no clustering solution comes close once preprocessing robustness is required
In [50]:
# Business-Tolerance Scenarios
BUSINESS_TOLERANCE_SCENARIOS = {
    'Strict': {'near_best_tolerance': 0.05, 'other_outcome_floor': 0.90},
    'Balanced': {'near_best_tolerance': 0.10, 'other_outcome_floor': 0.80},
    'Broad': {'near_best_tolerance': 0.20, 'other_outcome_floor': 0.70},
}
MINIMUM_SENSITIVITY_ARI = 0.70
METHOD_SIMPLICITY = {
    'RFM rules': 0, 'K-means': 1, 'Gaussian mixture': 2,
    'Ward clustering': 3, 'DBSCAN': 4, 'HDBSCAN': 5,
    'Spectral clustering': 6,
}

recommendation_pool = (
    sensitivity_candidates
    .merge(sensitivity_summary, on='solution_id', validate='one_to_one')
)
recommendation_pool['method_simplicity'] = recommendation_pool['method'].map(METHOD_SIMPLICITY)
recommendation_pool['sensitivity_review'] = (
    recommendation_pool['minimum_sensitivity_ari'].lt(MINIMUM_SENSITIVITY_ARI)
)
recommendation_pool['deployment_ready'] = (
    recommendation_pool['native_assignment'].eq('Yes')
    & recommendation_pool['noise_share'].le(MAXIMUM_NOISE_SHARE)
    & recommendation_pool['smallest_cluster_share'].ge(MINIMUM_CLUSTER_SHARE)
)

def select_under_business_tolerance(frame, near_best_tolerance, other_outcome_floor):
    eligible = frame.loc[frame['deployment_ready']].copy()
    if eligible.empty:
        return None, 0, 'No deployment-ready candidate'
    best_revenue = eligible['minimum_holdout_revenue_eta2'].max()
    best_activity = eligible['minimum_holdout_active_eta2'].max()
    revenue_near_best = eligible['minimum_holdout_revenue_eta2'].ge(
        best_revenue * (1 - near_best_tolerance)
    )
    activity_near_best = eligible['minimum_holdout_active_eta2'].ge(
        best_activity * (1 - near_best_tolerance)
    )
    revenue_floor = eligible['minimum_holdout_revenue_eta2'].ge(
        best_revenue * other_outcome_floor
    )
    activity_floor = eligible['minimum_holdout_active_eta2'].ge(
        best_activity * other_outcome_floor
    )
    sufficient = eligible.loc[
        (revenue_near_best & activity_floor)
        | (activity_near_best & revenue_floor)
    ].copy()
    selection_basis = 'Business-tolerance gates'
    if sufficient.empty:
        business_frontier = identify_pareto_efficient(
            eligible,
            maximize=['minimum_holdout_revenue_eta2', 'minimum_holdout_active_eta2'],
            minimize=[],
        )
        sufficient = eligible.loc[business_frontier].copy()
        selection_basis = 'Business-outcome Pareto frontier'
    selected = sufficient.sort_values(
        ['method_simplicity', 'cluster_count', 'evaluation_runtime_seconds', 'solution_id']
    ).iloc[0]
    return selected, len(sufficient), selection_basis

recommendation_records = []
for scenario_name, rules in BUSINESS_TOLERANCE_SCENARIOS.items():
    selected, sufficient_count, selection_basis = select_under_business_tolerance(
        recommendation_pool, **rules
    )
    recommendation_records.append({
        'business_scenario': scenario_name,
        'near_best_tolerance': rules['near_best_tolerance'],
        'other_outcome_floor': rules['other_outcome_floor'],
        'sufficient_candidates': sufficient_count,
        'recommended_solution_id': None if selected is None else selected['solution_id'],
        'recommended_method': None if selected is None else selected['method'],
        'selection_basis': selection_basis,
    })

recommendation_sensitivity = pd.DataFrame(recommendation_records)
display(
    recommendation_sensitivity.style.hide(axis='index').format({
        'near_best_tolerance': '{:.0%}',
        'other_outcome_floor': '{:.0%}',
        'sufficient_candidates': '{:,.0f}',
    })
)

Testable Segment Actions¶

  • Descriptive evidence was converted into experiments rather than claims about treatment effects (Table 31)
  • The two least active segments (49.7% of customers, 21.6% and 42.3% holdout-active) map to reactivation tests measured on incremental 90-day purchase rate
  • The three more active segments map to recognition and early-access tests measured on incremental revenue per contacted customer
  • Guardrails are stated alongside each hypothesis: opt-out rate, contact fatigue, discount cost, and margin
  • Campaign tests should use randomized holdouts wherever practical; none of these hypotheses is supported by the study itself
In [52]:
# Testable Segment Actions
recommended_profile = segment_profiles.loc[
    segment_profiles['solution_id'].eq(recommended_solution_id)
].copy()

def assign_action_hypothesis(row):
    if row['holdout_active_rate'] >= recommended_profile['holdout_active_rate'].median():
        return pd.Series({
            'evidence_pattern': 'Higher future activity',
            'testable_hypothesis': 'Recognition or early-access treatment increases repeat revenue',
            'primary_outcome': 'Incremental revenue per contacted customer',
            'guardrail': 'Opt-out rate and discount cost',
        })
    if row['median_recency'] >= recommended_profile['median_recency'].median():
        return pd.Series({
            'evidence_pattern': 'Longer time since purchase',
            'testable_hypothesis': 'A reactivation message increases the return-to-purchase rate',
            'primary_outcome': 'Incremental 90-day purchase rate',
            'guardrail': 'Contact fatigue and margin',
        })
    return pd.Series({
        'evidence_pattern': 'Developing relationship',
        'testable_hypothesis': 'Relevant product discovery increases purchase breadth',
        'primary_outcome': 'Incremental unique products purchased',
        'guardrail': 'Unsubscribe rate and margin',
    })

action_hypotheses = pd.concat(
    [
        recommended_profile[['cluster', 'customers', 'customer_share', 'holdout_active_rate', 'holdout_revenue_lift']].reset_index(drop=True),
        recommended_profile.apply(assign_action_hypothesis, axis=1).reset_index(drop=True),
    ],

)

Refresh & Monitoring¶

  • Production use requires a documented feature window, stored score cutoffs, versioned assignment logic, and recurring drift review (Table 32)
  • Five monitors defined with explicit review triggers and responses: assignment coverage, segment-size drift, assignment confidence, segment outcome stability, and campaign incrementality
  • Monitoring is designed to detect when the original segment interpretation or the assignment process is no longer reliable

        'response': 'Revalidate interpretation and business usefulness',
    },
    {
        'monitor': 'Campaign incrementality', 'cadence': 'Each experiment',
        'review_trigger': 'Treatment effect is absent or guardrail deteriorates',
        'response': 'Stop, revise, or narrow the segment treatment',
    },
])
display(monitoring_register.style.hide(axis='index').set_properties(**{'text-align': 'left'}))
monitor cadence review_trigger response
Assignment coverage Each scoring run More than 1% of eligible customers unassigned Inspect feature completeness and scoring logic
Segment-size drift Monthly Any segment changes by more than 20% relative to baseline share Review feature and customer-mix drift before campaign use
Assignment confidence Monthly Median margin falls below 80% of development baseline Inspect overlap and consider model refresh
Segment outcome stability Quarterly Rank ordering or material outcome differences no longer persist Revalidate interpretation and business usefulness
Campaign incrementality Each experiment Treatment effect is absent or guardrail deteriorates Stop, revise, or narrow the segment treatment

Final Decision Validation¶

  • Six checks confirmed the recommendation is reproducible from the stated rules, stays connected to both baseline methods, and has complete action and monitoring outputs (Table 33)

12Study Limitations

  • Only three of seven families reached business evaluation: DBSCAN collapsed to fewer than two clusters and HDBSCAN exceeded 55% noise at every setting tested, so the study reports on those grids rather than on the methods in general
  • The deployment gate requires native new-customer assignment, which structurally excludes Ward, DBSCAN, and spectral clustering regardless of their evidence
  • Absolute differentiation is modest: the selected solution accounts for 5.8% of holdout revenue variance and 26.2% of holdout activity variance, so the segments rank customers well but explain a minority of the variation
  • The business-tolerance gates are relative to the best available candidate, with no absolute floor, so the rule always returns a recommendation even when the whole field is weak
  • η² rises mechanically with group count; the Pareto step trades this off against cluster count rather than correcting the bias
  • Evaluation runtime enters the Pareto comparison, so the shortlist carries some machine dependence
  • Stability refits hold density parameters at absolute values on a smaller sample, which is conservative toward DBSCAN and HDBSCAN
  • The holdout was used to compare candidates and is therefore a validation period, not an untouched final test
  • Segment definitions reflect one retailer's 2009-2011 giftware transactions; 22.8% of rows carry no customer ID and sit outside customer-level modeling entirely
  • All findings are associations in historical purchasing behavior; no causal effect of segment membership or campaign treatment is estimated

13Conclusions & Method Selection

  • Compared seven segmentation approaches across 52 configurations on identical customer data, judged on statistical structure, stability, out-of-time business differentiation, interpretability, deployability, and preprocessing sensitivity
Statistical Evidence.
  • 16 of 52 configurations cleared the initial gates; Ward, DBSCAN, and HDBSCAN cleared none
  • K-means and Gaussian mixture reached the highest stability (0.940), with RFM rules close behind (0.889)
  • Internal indices proved unreliable as a selection signal: DBSCAN posted the best silhouette (0.482) on degenerate one-and-two-cluster solutions
Business Evidence.
  • RFM rules led every out-of-time measure except holdout revenue: activity 0.262, orders 0.223, product breadth 0.204
  • Gaussian mixture at four components edged the baseline on holdout revenue alone (0.062 against 0.058), a gap well inside the bootstrap intervals
  • The best K-means configuration trailed the baseline on both headline outcomes
Operational Fit.
  • K-means separates more features than RFM (seven against four) and carries a far higher assignment margin (0.339 against 0.069)
  • RFM holds a decisive operational advantage in segment size: no group below 14.5% of customers, against 1.6% to 1.7% for the K-means configurations
  • Both support direct new-customer assignment; RFM needs no stored model artifact beyond the score cutoffs
Preprocessing Sensitivity.
  • This is where the clustering solutions failed: worst-case agreement with the primary specification ranged from 0.007 to 0.177 adjusted Rand index
  • A segmentation whose customer assignments dissolve when capping or log transformation changes cannot be deployed, whatever its differentiation scores
  • RFM assignments were unchanged (1.000), because monotone transformations cannot alter rank-based rules
Final Method Selection.
  • RFM rules with five segments selected as the preferred method
  • Only candidate to clear the business-tolerance gates under strict, balanced, and broad settings
  • Strongest out-of-time behavioral differentiation, largest minimum segment, lowest refresh effort, and no sensitivity to preprocessing choices
  • The trade-off accepted: weaker geometric separation and fewer high-contrast features than K-means, in exchange for assignments that hold still
  • Six clustering families did not repay their complexity against a properly constructed baseline, which is the result the study was designed to be able to detect
  • Segment value should be confirmed through controlled campaign testing before broad operational adoption

Key decisions

  1. 1Give every method the same feature matrixShared Matrix · seven behaviors, one pipeline
  2. 2Score RFM on values, never on row orderCandidate Methods · tied customers share a score
  3. 3Judge segments on later behavior, not fitBusiness Evidence · six months held back
  4. 4Require assignments to survive preprocessingSensitivity · clustering ARI fell to 0.007
